To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dynamics of available soil P depends on the dynamics of phosphate ions in a central pool of the available soil P.

(i), available soil phosphate can be characterized by five compartments which are directly branched one on the other and which are characterized by the time required to release their phosphate ions to the soil solution, (ii) the quantity of P in each compartment decreases ineluctabley with continuous cropping without P application and increases with P application, (iii) the intensity factor of each compartment increases with P application.

available soil P can be described as a pool of phosphate ions which are in a steady state with soil particles and with the soil solution, that this pool is characterized by an intensity factor which is the rate of transfer of phosphate ions from soil particles to the soil solution, by a quantity factor which is the quantity of phosphate ions in this pool, by a capacity factor which is the maximum quantity of phosphate ions which could be transferred from the solid phase to the soil solution in one day and by a time factor
In summary, our research is concerned with
the description of the dynamics of P in soils, using isotopic techniques, with special attention to the description and the determination of available soil P.
the description of the available soil P as a system of five pools of phosphate ion, with increasing rates of transfer.
the study of the P dynamics in soils, with a view to understanding and controlling it.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
available soil P is a system with many compartments which are characterized by the time required to transfer phosphate ions from soil particles to the soil solution.

the intensity and the quantity factors of the available soil P pool depend on the quantity and type of P fertilizer and crop residues applied to soil, on the quantity of P removed from soil with the crops and on the capacity of the soil to retain P.

the intensity and quantity factor of available soil P, which characterize the directly available phosphate ions, depend essentially on the soil P fertility and on its capacity for phosphate fixation, and that the absolute value of the increase in these two factors after a P application depends essentially on the type of P applied and the soil P fertility level before the application.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
available soil P is the quantity of P in a soil, which can be taken up by plants in one year, if the soil has no P application.

the intensity and quantity factor of available soil P, and consequently its availability, depend mainly on the quantity of directly available phosphate ions in soils and on the quantity of phosphate ions fixed on the solid phase of soil.

(i), for a given soil, the quantity of available P is a function of the quantity of P in the soil, of the P uptake by plants and of the intensity factor (ii), for a given quantity of available P, the intensity factor depends on the P uptake by the plants and on the quantity of P contained in the central pool of available P (iii) the quantity of P applied on the soil does not always increase the available soil P.
The main takeaway from our work is that
available soil P can be considered as a system with a central compartment which contains only phosphate ions which are directly available to plants.
the dynamics of P in the soil-plant system can be described by the intensity, quantity and the capacity factors, which are derived from isotopic data.
, for agronomic purposes, the quantity and intensity factors are more important than the capacity factor.
